A Tale of Two Cities. This novel was serialized from 1859 to 1860 and stands as Charles Dickens's historical novel of the French Revolution, moving between the cities of London and Paris. It opens with one of the most famous lines in English literature: "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times." That paradox captures the entire spirit of the work, weaving together personal love and redemption against the backdrop of revolution. At the center of the story is Sydney Carton, a dissolute lawyer who bears a striking physical resemblance to the French aristocrat Charles Darnay. Carton redeems himself through a final act of sacrifice, dying on the guillotine in Darnay's place, speaking the novel's closing words: "It is a far, far better thing that I do, than I have ever done." Charles Darnay himself has renounced his French title and the oppressive world of aristocracy to live quietly in England, representing the conscience of his class. The heroine is Lucie Manette, whose father was long confined to the Bastille as a political prisoner. Her love becomes the emotional center that draws both Carton and Darnay toward redemption. Against them stands Madame Defarge, a female revolutionary who knits coded messages that list the names of those marked for execution. She embodies the implacable violence of the Revolution itself. Set during the Terror and the storming of the Bastille, the novel balances the possibility of individual redemption against the overwhelming force of historical violence.
